blocks.explanation:
The factors 8, 7, 6, 5 are consecutive and go down.
Plan: complete the product down to 1 by multiplying top and bottom by \(4!\).
steps:
Given: \(8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5\)
To find: the same number written with factorials.
Method: A product of consecutive numbers from \(a\) down to \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a!}{(b - 1)!}\): multiply by the missing numbers \((b - 1)(b - 2) \cdots 1\) on top and bottom.

Multiply and divide by \(4!\)
\[8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 = \dfrac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4!}{4!}\]
Why: Multiplying and dividing by the same number does not change the value; \(4! = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1\) supplies the missing factors.

Recognise the factorial on top
\[= \dfrac{8!}{4!}\]
Why: \(8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 8!\).

Check
\[8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 = 1680\]
\[\dfrac{40320}{24} = 1680 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Both forms give the same number.

blocks.explanation:
Consecutive factors from 15 down to 11.
Plan: the next number would be 10, so multiply top and bottom by \(10!\).
steps:
Given: \(15 \cdot 14 \cdot 13 \cdot 12 \cdot 11\)
To find: the factorial form.
Method: A product of consecutive numbers from \(a\) down to \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a!}{(b - 1)!}\): multiply by the missing numbers \((b - 1)(b - 2) \cdots 1\) on top and bottom.

Multiply and divide by \(10!\)
\[= \dfrac{15 \cdot 14 \cdot 13 \cdot 12 \cdot 11 \cdot 10!}{10!}\]
Why: The product stops at 11, so the missing part is 10 down to 1.

Write the top as a factorial
\[= \dfrac{15!}{10!}\]
Why: 15 down to 1 is \(15!\).

Check
\[15 \cdot 14 \cdot 13 \cdot 12 \cdot 11 = 360360\]
\[\dfrac{15!}{10!} = 360360 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Same value.

blocks.explanation:
Consecutive factors from 19 down to 16.
Plan: the next number is 15, so use \(15!\).
steps:
Given: \(19 \cdot 18 \cdot 17 \cdot 16\)
To find: the factorial form.
Method: A product of consecutive numbers from \(a\) down to \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a!}{(b - 1)!}\): multiply by the missing numbers \((b - 1)(b - 2) \cdots 1\) on top and bottom.

Multiply and divide by \(15!\)
\[= \dfrac{19 \cdot 18 \cdot 17 \cdot 16 \cdot 15!}{15!}\]
Why: The factors 15 down to 1 are missing.

Write the top as a factorial
\[= \dfrac{19!}{15!}\]
Why: 19 down to 1 is \(19!\).

Check
\[19 \cdot 18 \cdot 17 \cdot 16 = 93024\]
\[\dfrac{19!}{15!} = 93024 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Same value. Count check: \(19 - 15 = 4\) factors.

blocks.explanation:
Both the top and the bottom are runs of consecutive numbers.
Plan: write each run in factorial form separately, then combine.
steps:
Given: \(\dfrac{11 \cdot 10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7}{5 \cdot 4}\)
To find: the factorial form.
Method: A product of consecutive numbers from \(a\) down to \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a!}{(b - 1)!}\): multiply by the missing numbers \((b - 1)(b - 2) \cdots 1\) on top and bottom.

Top in factorial form
\[11 \cdot 10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 = \dfrac{11!}{6!}\]
Why: The run stops at 7, so the missing part is 6 down to 1.

Bottom in factorial form
\[5 \cdot 4 = \dfrac{5!}{3!}\]
Why: The run stops at 4, so the missing part is 3 down to 1.

Divide
\[\dfrac{11!/6!}{5!/3!} = \dfrac{11!\,3!}{6!\,5!}\]
Why: Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal, so \(3!\) moves to the top.

Check
\[\dfrac{55440}{20} = 2772\]
\[\dfrac{11! \cdot 6}{720 \cdot 120} = 2772 \;\checkmark\]
Why: \(11 \cdot 10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 = 55440\), and both forms give 2772.

blocks.explanation: The bottom is already \(5!\). Plan: write the top as a factorial quotient and combine.
steps:
Given: \(\dfrac{10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1}\)
To find: the factorial form.
Method: A product of consecutive numbers from \(a\) down to \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a!}{(b - 1)!}\): multiply by the missing numbers \((b - 1)(b - 2) \cdots 1\) on top and bottom.

Write top and bottom
\[10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 = \dfrac{10!}{5!}\]
\[5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 5!\]
Why: The top run stops at 6; the bottom goes all the way to 1.

Combine
\[\dfrac{10!/5!}{5!} = \dfrac{10!}{5!\,5!}\]
Why: Dividing by \(5!\) again puts a second \(5!\) in the denominator.

Check
\[\dfrac{30240}{120} = 252\]
\[\dfrac{3628800}{120 \cdot 120} = 252 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Same value.

blocks.explanation: The bottom is \(5!\); the top runs from 50 down to 47. Plan: as in (v).
steps:
Given: \(\dfrac{50 \cdot 49 \cdot 48 \cdot 47}{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1}\)
To find: the factorial form.
Method: A product of consecutive numbers from \(a\) down to \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a!}{(b - 1)!}\): multiply by the missing numbers \((b - 1)(b - 2) \cdots 1\) on top and bottom.

Write top and bottom
\[50 \cdot 49 \cdot 48 \cdot 47 = \dfrac{50!}{46!}\]
\[5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 5!\]
Why: The top run stops at 47, so 46 down to 1 is missing.

Combine
\[= \dfrac{50!}{5!\,46!}\]
Why: \(46!\) and \(5!\) are both in the denominator.

Check
\[\dfrac{5527200}{120} = 46060\]
\[\dfrac{50!}{5!\,46!} = 46060 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Same value (checked with exact arithmetic).

blocks.explanation:
Now the numbers are algebraic, but the idea is the same: consecutive factors going down.
Plan: the next factor would be \(n - 4\), so divide by \((n - 4)!\).
steps:
Given: \(n(n - 1)(n - 2)(n - 3)\)
To find: the factorial form.
Method: A product of consecutive numbers from \(a\) down to \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a!}{(b - 1)!}\): multiply by the missing numbers \((b - 1)(b - 2) \cdots 1\) on top and bottom.

Multiply and divide by \((n - 4)!\)
\[= \dfrac{n(n - 1)(n - 2)(n - 3)(n - 4)!}{(n - 4)!}\]
Why: The run stops at \(n - 3\); the missing part is \((n - 4)(n - 5) \cdots 1 = (n - 4)!\).

Write the top as a factorial
\[= \dfrac{n!}{(n - 4)!}\]
Why: \(n\) down to 1 is \(n!\).

Check with a number
\[n = 6:\ 6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 360\]
\[\dfrac{6!}{2!} = \dfrac{720}{2} = 360 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Putting in a value tests the algebra.

blocks.explanation:
Consecutive factors from \(n + 2\) down to \(n - 1\).
Plan: the next factor is \(n - 2\), so divide by \((n - 2)!\).
steps:
Given: \((n + 2)(n + 1)n(n - 1)\)
To find: the factorial form.
Method: A product of consecutive numbers from \(a\) down to \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a!}{(b - 1)!}\): multiply by the missing numbers \((b - 1)(b - 2) \cdots 1\) on top and bottom.

Multiply and divide by \((n - 2)!\)
\[= \dfrac{(n + 2)(n + 1)n(n - 1)(n - 2)!}{(n - 2)!}\]
Why: The missing part below \(n - 1\) is \((n - 2)!\).

Write the top as a factorial
\[= \dfrac{(n + 2)!}{(n - 2)!}\]
Why: The top now runs from \(n + 2\) down to 1.

Check with a number
\[n = 3:\ 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 120\]
\[\dfrac{5!}{1!} = 120 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Same value.

blocks.explanation: Top: consecutive factors from \(n + 3\) down to \(n\); bottom: \(5!\). Plan: as in (vii), then divide by \(5!\).
steps:
Given: \(\dfrac{(n + 3)(n + 2)(n + 1)n}{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1}\)
To find: the factorial form.
Method: A product of consecutive numbers from \(a\) down to \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a!}{(b - 1)!}\): multiply by the missing numbers \((b - 1)(b - 2) \cdots 1\) on top and bottom.

Top in factorial form
\[(n + 3)(n + 2)(n + 1)n = \dfrac{(n + 3)!}{(n - 1)!}\]
Why: The run stops at \(n\), so the missing part is \((n - 1)!\).

Divide by the bottom
\[\dfrac{(n + 3)!}{(n - 1)!\,5!}\]
Why: \(5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 5!\).

Check with a number
\[n = 2:\ \dfrac{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2}{120} = 1\]
\[\dfrac{5!}{1!\,5!} = 1 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Same value.

blocks.prompt: 4 (x) Write in the factorial form: \(n(n - 1)(n - 2) \ldots (n - r + 2)\)
blocks.explanation:
Consecutive factors from \(n\) down to \(n - r + 2\).
Plan: the next factor after \(n - r + 2\) is \(n - r + 1\); divide by \((n - r + 1)!\).
steps:
Given: \(n(n - 1)(n - 2) \cdots (n - r + 2)\)
To find: the factorial form.
Method: A product of consecutive numbers from \(a\) down to \(b\) is \(\dfrac{a!}{(b - 1)!}\): multiply by the missing numbers \((b - 1)(b - 2) \cdots 1\) on top and bottom.

Find the missing part
\[(n - r + 2) - 1 = n - r + 1\]
Why: Each factor is one less than the one before, so the first missing factor is \(n - r + 1\).

Multiply and divide by \((n - r + 1)!\)
\[= \dfrac{n(n - 1) \cdots (n - r + 2)(n - r + 1)!}{(n - r + 1)!}\]
\[= \dfrac{n!}{(n - r + 1)!}\]
Why: The top now runs from \(n\) down to 1, which is \(n!\).

Check with numbers
\[n = 6,\ r = 3:\ 6 \cdot 5 = 30\]
\[\dfrac{6!}{4!} = 30 \;\checkmark\]
Why: With \(n = 6\), \(r = 3\) the last factor is \(n - r + 2 = 5\). Note: this product has \(r - 1\) factors, so it equals \({}^{n}P_{r-1}\).
